description: Capital of the autonomous community of Catalonia. Spain’s second largest city. Population: 1,670,000 (Barcelonais and Barcelonaises) The name Barcelona immediately brings to mind Antoni Gaudí, the architectural genius who left his mark on the city in the shape of the Park Güell, Casa Batlló and, above all, by initiating the construction of the majestic Sagrada Família, on which work will continue with the tallest of its 18 towers set to be inaugurated next June.. Sports fans have been captivated the historic successes of FC Barcelona for almost as long. The iconic football club has won the Spanish championship 28 times and been crowned European champions five times thanks to the exploits of Johann Cruyff, Diego Maradona, Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal, who are among the many renowned players to have worn the Catalan club’s famous blaugrana (blue and red) colours. While Barça’s handball and basketball teams have also shone on the international stage, the Catalan capital’s defining sporting moment was the hosting of the 1992 Olympic Games, which helped to reshape the city’s geography. The 25th Olympic Games is remembered for Michael Jordan and Magic Johnson’s Dream Team and for French athlete Marie-José Pérec’s first Olympic title in the 400 metres, while its focal point was the Montjuïc hill, which the Tour de France riders will become very familiar with during the opening two stages in July 2026.

Stage town for the 6th time Capital of the autonomous community of Catalonia. Spain’s second largest city Population: 1,670,000 (Barcelonais and Barcelonaises) Spain’s second city was the birthplace of the country’s oldest stage race. Created in 1911, the Volta a Catalunya was launched by the weekly sports newspaper El Mundo Deportivo, which later became a daily. Mariano Cañardo holds the record for Tour of Catalonia titles (1928-29-30-32-35-36-39), although he only won a single stage of the Tour de France, in 1937 at Ax-les-Thermes. However, two of his successors managed to win the Tour de France in the same year as the Volta. Miguel Induráin achieved this feat in 1991 and 1992, while Tadej Pogačar won the final stage on the hill at Montjuïc during his victory in 2024.

A new stage town Commune in Pyrénées-Orientales (66) Population: 600 (Anglois and Angloises) In summer, this Pyrenean resort is very popular with mountain bikers, who gather there for downhill races. In 2022, it also hosted a stage finish of the Route d’Occitanie, when Canadian Michael Woods took the lead in the overall classification after taking the day’s honours ahead of Carlos Rodríguez. Although the Tour de France peloton has never visited Les Angles, neighbouring Font-Romeu has hosted two stage starts: in 1968, when the riders headed for Albi, and in 1976, when the stage went to Saint-Gaudens.

Stage town for the 8th time Prefecture of Ariège (09) Population: 9,800 (Fuxéens and Fuxéennes) The five finishes in Foix have rewarded audacious racers. This was the case in 2008 when Kurt-Asle Arvesen outsprinted his last two breakaway companions, Alessandro Ballan and Martin Elmiger. In 2012, Luis León Sánchez rode to a solo victory after jumping away from the breakaway group. On Bastille Day in 2017, Warren Barguil was the fastest of a quartet that also included Alberto Contador, Nairo Quintana and Mikel Landa. Two years later, the finish line was on the high ridge above town at Prat dAlbis, where Simon Yates was the victor. The last winner here, in 2022, was Canadian Hugo Houle, who made a 40km solo break to claim what remains Quebec’s only Tour success.

Stage city for the 77th time Prefecture of Pyrénées-Atlantiques (64) Population: 77,600 (Palois and Paloises); 162,000 within the 32 communes comprising the Pau Béarn Pyrénées municipality Pau’s status as the Tour’s base camp either before or after climbs in the Pyrenees began in 1930. Its location lends itself to every type of stage, which is backed up by the list of winners in Henry IV’s home town, who range from climbers like René Vietto and Fausto Coppi to breakaway specialists such as Pierrick Fédrigo and to sprinters like Sean Kelly, Robbie McEwen, Arnaud Démare and, in 2024, Jasper Philipsen. In 2019, the capital of Béarn celebrated the centenary of the Yellow Jersey, when Julian Alaphilippe honoured it with a masterful performance.

A new stage town Commune in Hautes-Pyrénées (65) Population: 350 (Gavarniens and Gavarniennes, Gédrois and Gédroises) The merger of Gavarnie and Gèdre in 2016 resulted in the formation of the largest commune in Occitanie and the one of the biggest in France in terms of surface area. The area’s reputation is assured by the Cirque de Gavarnie, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The ski resort made its debut on the cycling scene In 2022 when it hosted a stage finish of the Ronde de l’Isard. Lenny Martinez finished second behind Spain’s Samuel Fernández, while Norway’s Johannes Staune-Mittet took the leader’s jersey, which he held for the rest of the race.

Stage town for the 82nd time Prefecture of Gironde (33) and capital of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region Population: 266,000 (Bordelais and Bordelaises) The prefecture of Nouvelle-Aquitaine is second only to Paris in terms of Tour visits and, based on the list of winners of the 81 finishes since 1903, just about rivals it as the capital of sprinting. The greatest specialists have won either at the Lescure velodrome or on Bordeaux’s quaysides, including Rik Van Looy, André Darrigade, Walter Godefroot, Freddy Maertens, Danny Van Poppel, Erik Zabel, Mark Cavendish and, on the last visit in 2023, Jasper Philipsen. However, the record holder for stage victories in the city is Eddy Merckx, who won here four times, including three time trial successes.

Stage town for the 5th time Sub-prefecture of Dordogne (24) Population: 26,900 (Bergeracois and Bergeracoises) Although the hero of Edmond Rostand’s play has no direct connection with the town, Cyrano has nevertheless been immortalised with a statue in a square in Bergerac’s historic centre. Apart from the time trials associated with Périgueux, the town has hosted two Tour stage finishes. In 2014, Lithuania’s Ramunas Navardauskas required equal amounts of flair and power to catch the peloton out with a masterful attack 13 kilometres from the finish. In 2017, Marcel Kittel’s unmatchable speed enabled him to clinch the 13th of his 14 Tour victories.

A new stage town Sub-prefecture of Corrèze (19) Population: 9,200 (Ussellois and Usselloises) A new town on the Tour route, Ussel will become the sixth to host the race in the department of Corrèze, alongside the likes of Sarran, Brive and Tulle. The town is, however, already used to welcoming the professional peloton, for Paris-Corrèze, for example, which finished here in 2003 when Nicolas Fritsch was first across the line. Ussel has also seen Tour de France stage-winners celebrating victory: Francis Campaner was the victor here in 1975, followed by Mariano Martinez in 1978, Jean-François Bernard in 1985 and, most recently, David Moncoutié in 2001. Turning to the women, Marianne Vos was the victor the last time the Tour Féminin en Limousin paused in Ussel in 2012.

Stage town for the fourth time Mountain resort in Cantal (15) attached to the commune of Laveissière Population: 540 (Valagnons and Valagnonnes) The ski resort built at the foot of the Plomb du Cantal welcomed the Tour de France peloton for the finish of the longest stage of the 1975 edition, won by Michel Pollentier after 260km of racing. In 2016, Greg Van Avermaet won at Le Lioran and also took the Yellow Jersey. In 2024, Jonas Vingegaard gave his supporters hope by winning a sprint duel with Tadej Pogačar for the first time. However, the Slovenian wasn’t caught out again as he went on to seal overall victory in Nice.

Stage town for the 4th time Prefecture of Nièvre (58) Population: 33,200 (Neversois and Neversoises) Ideally placed on the diagonal route of “the race to the sun”, Nièvre’s prefecture is one of the towns most frequented by Paris-Nice. Coming early on in the race, it’s tended to favour sprinters, including Mario Cipollini (1992-93), Tom Steels (1998), Jaan Kirsipuu (1999-2000) and Gert Steegmans on the last bunch finish in 2008. However, last spring, a team time trial run between the motor-racing circuit and the town was won by the Visma | Lease a Bike line-up that featured Matteo Jorgenson, who went on to win the race. The Tour hasn’t been here since 2003, when Alessandro Petacchi won the bunch sprint.

Stage city for the 6th time Sub-prefecture of Saône-et-Loire (71) Population: 44,600 (Chalonnais and Chalonnaises) French sports fans have followed the rise of Elan Chalon, two-time winners of the French basketball championship (2012, 2017). When it comes to cycling, historians will highlight British racing pioneer Brian Robinson’s victory here in 1959 after a long solo breakaway. On the Tour’s next finish in Chalon, in 1988, Thierry Marie won his second stage by outsmarting the sprinters in the final kilometre. Dylan Groenewegen, however, wasn’t caught napping when he drew on his finishing speed to claim the fourth of his six Tour stages in 2019.

Stage town for the 33rd time Prefecture of the Territory of Belfort (90) Population: 46,000 (Belfortains and Belfortaines) Hailing from nearby Colmar, Auguste Bartholdi transformed his neighbouring town by sculpting the Lion of Belfort. Much later, in 2012 to be exact, the animal passed on its strength and courage to a young cyclist whose talent was beginning to stand out. After a start in Belfort, Thibaut Pinot won his first Tour stage at Porrentruy at the age of 22. Since then, the peloton has set off twice beneath the gaze of the stone beast: in 2019, when Dylan Groenewegen took victory in Chalon-sur-Saône, and in 2023, when “Tibopino” produced his last thrilling performance prior to Tadej Pogačar’s success at Le Markstein.

Stage site for the second time Mountain resort and summit (1,265m) in the Vosges mountains in Haut-Rhin (68) attached to the commune of Oderen Population: 1,250 (Odernois and Odernoises) During the 1980s, two rounds of the Alpine Skiing World Cup were organised in the Vosges resort. Long after Swedish legend Ingemar Stenmark had tasted success here, another champion made her mark at Le Markstein during the 2022 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift: Annemiek van Vleuten took the Yellow Jersey here and effectively tied up the overall title such was her advantage at the line. And in 2023, Tadej Pogačar made it a point of honour to win here in the final days of a Tour that was slipping away from him, much to the consternation of Thibaut Pinot, who was denied the victory in front of his home fans that he’d been dreaming of in his last Tour.

A new stage site Pass (1,497m) in the Bornes massif in the Alps in Haute-Savoie (74), attached to the commune of Brison (or Brizon) Population: 470 (Brisonniers and Brisonnières) The Tour de l’Avenir is the race where young talent is discovered, often highlighting riders destined for a prestigious future. This was the case at Plateau de Solaison, which featured on the route of the 2014 edition of this under-23 race. At the end of the stage’s final climb, the top five included Miguel Ángel López, Pierre Latour and Giulio Ciccone. The Critérium du Dauphiné then sent its champions to battle it out there on the final stage in 2017, when Jakob Fuglsang took the opportunity to remove the leader’s jersey from Richie Porte’s shoulders. In 2022, the final day was dominated by Jumbo-Visma: the stage went to Jonas Vingegaard and overall victory to Primož Roglič after the pair had finished hand in hand.

Stage town for the 10th time Sub-prefecture of Haute-Savoie (74) Population: 37,700 (Thononais and Thononaises) The second largest town in Haute-Savoie hosted the Tour de France for the first time in 1955. When it set off from the shores of Lake Geneva, the peloton wasn’t completely aware of the extent of Charly Gaul’s ability. He attacked not long after the start and then went solo on the Galibier before triumphing in Briançon with a lead of almost 14 minutes. The 23-year-old Luxembourger finished third on the podium in Paris, behind Louison Bobet and Jean Brankart. In terms of stage finishes, the last one in Thonon was in 1981, when Sean Kelly won in a sprint.

Stage town for the second time Commune in Isère (38) Population: 21,900 (Voironnais and Voironnaises) This commune in Isère is primarily renowned for the famous Chartreuse liqueur made by the Carthusian monks, whose secret recipe has been kept for several centuries, but it’s also the birthplace of Olympic and world discus champion Melina Robert-Michon, as well as 2003 world handball champion Véronique Pecqueux-Rolland. Set close to Grenoble, Voiron has witnessed victories by two very significant Belgian Classics riders in the Critérium du Dauphiné: Stan Ockers in 1956 and Wout van Aert in 2019.

Stage town for the sixth time Mountain resort in Hautes-Alpes (05) attached to the commune of Orcières Population: 670 (Orcatus and Orcatuses) The best-remembered Tour finish in Orcières was the first one in 1971, when Luis Ocaña imposed himself on his rivals. The driving force in a relentlessly fast breakaway, the Spaniard rode the last 60 kilometres alone and finished almost nine minutes ahead of Eddy Merckx. The margin seemed decisive at the time, but the duel between the two big favourites ultimately ended when the Spaniard crashed in the Pyrenees and abandoned the race. This anecdote may provide Primož Roglič with food for thought, as he also won in the Hautes-Alpes resort early on in the 2020 Tour only to suffer brutal disappointment in that edition’s final time trial at La Planche des Belles Filles.

Stage town for the 32nd time Mountain resort in Isère (38) attached to the commune of Huez Population: 1,300 (D’Huizats and D’Huizates) In 1952, Fausto Coppi launched the fabled history of mountain finishes by taking the Yellow Jersey at the top of the now famous road with 21 hairpins. Thanks to Joop Zoetemelk, Hennie Kuiper and Peter Winnen each winning here twice, it earned the nickname “Dutch mountain”, before the Italians returned to the fore once again with Gianni Bugno and then Marco Pantani. As for the French, Laurent Fignon gained some valuable ground here in 1984 during his duel with Bernard Hinault. Two years later, Hinault became the first Frenchman to win here in a famous finish that also saw him hand over power to his American teammate Greg LeMond.

Stage town for the 33rd time Mountain resort in Isère (38) attached to the commune of Huez Population: 1,300 (D’Huizats and D’Huizates) This is a mountain where success goes in cycles. The French successors to Bernard Hinault’s win emerged in this century, Pierre Rolland picking up the torch in 2011, followed, in 2013, by Christophe Riblon. Thibaut Pinot then achieved one of his greatest successes here in 2015. Since then, the ski station has been under British control on the days the Tour has visited. Geraint Thomas (2018) and then Tom Pidcock (2022) both celebrated victory at Alpe d’Huez. Two years later, the Dutch flag was raised again by Demi Vollering at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, although she was beaten in the final overall classification by Kasia Niewiadoma by just four seconds.

51st finish on the Champs-Élysées Capital of France and the Île-de-France region Commune-department and prefecture (75) Population: 2,120,000 (Parisiens and Parisiennes) Over the centuries, the French capital has earned unrivalled prestige, making it the world’s leading tourist destination. Its success is due as much to the majesty of its monuments – from Cathedral of Notre-Dame to the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre Museum and the Arc de Triomphe – as to the cultural vibrancy that enlivens it and the elusive Parisian chic that continues to fascinate. The City of Light has also established itself as one of the world’s major sporting venues, thanks to regular events such as the Roland-Garros tennis tournament and the final stage of the Tour de France... and, of course, the organisation of the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the summer of 2024, when innovations such as the holding the opening ceremony in the heart of the city and having a marathon open to all helped to make sporting history.
